newsitem.title: CHINA: INTERVIEW - Hong Kong to stay China's gold gateway.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Hong Kong to stay China's gold gateway.

text.p: Hong Kong will be the gateway for gold trade with China long after the colony returns to the mainland, and a source of expertise and financing as a Chinese market develops, a gold industry executive said on Thursday.

China is unlikely to open its gold market before the end of this century, and it poses no long term threat to the thriving Hong Kong market, said Raymond Chan Fat Chu, president of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society.
"I don't think the Chinese are eager to open up the gold market in the next one or two years," Chan, who is also chairman of Tem Fat Hing Fung, told Reuters.
"The worry is behind the yuan's convertibility and the trend of the yuan if they (Chinese authorities) open up the gold market," he said in an interview.
Instead, China is effectively strangling the development of the gold industry by setting a retail gold price of close to $500 per ounce, he said.
By contrast, bullion was quoted in Hong Kong at midday at $344.80/345.30 an ounce.
China's authorities should open a jewellery mart, a fully integrated centre where gold is refined and made into jewellery for wholesale, saving insurance and transport costs, Chan said.
This concept had already been put into practice in Malaysia, financed with gold loans, he said, and was helping Malaysia to become one of the world's major gold exporters.

While the Penang exchange quotes a gold price, he said, this need not be a feature of a similar exchange in China, which could instead quote a central bank-set price and give a spread on jewellery quotations.
"When they get used to this, they will see how the jewellery industry improves. And when it does, the Chinese government will slowly grant licences to people who can offer gold," Chan said.
This was unlikely to happen before the next century, he said.
"In the meantime, Hong Kong remains the entrance and exit, the door to China for gold. The Hong Kong gold market will flourish," he said.

"When they open, they will need risk management, manufacturing experience, gold loans. We can be a window for them to get money, we can quote them gold loans, we can provide them with financing to speed up the development of the mining industry and then on to the jewellery industry.
"So Hong Kong will stay as it is," he said.
Once the Chinese gold market has developed -- most likely based in Shanghai -- it will provide a hedging and arbitraging opportunity by quoting in yuan, he said.
"They will definitely not quote U.S. dollars, they will quote yuan per gram. And this will create a very good arbitrage, very good hedging opportunity, for the worldwide bullion market," Chan said.
"So there will be three-way hedging, yuan-per-gram in Shanghai, U.S. dollars in London/New York and Hong Kong dollars in Hong Kong.

"It is a pity that China does not have a gold market. It is a pity that they don't have a gold quotation because they have everything -- they have integration from primary industry, secondary industry through to retail. They just need to put it all together," he said.
